shinyOAuth protocol quality: implementation plan

Steering-agent review and handoff (2026-11-18). Author: the separate Codex steering/review agent, at the user’s request. Reviewed clean checkout 43dd6d80488bae74010e3759017034af068fdce6, the implementation, retained reports, pinned upstream plan sources and current OIDF instructions. The user asked this agent to evaluate the implementation agent’s work and add these notes so the implementation agent can pick them up. This section preserves the execution history below; it records recommendations and review evidence, not completed implementation changes.

The existing approach should continue: real browser flows through public package APIs, exact suite module/variant matching, specific application rejection evidence, verified worker execution and explicit fixture limitations. Keep the separate suite verdict and application checks. During this review, all 6,682 evidence regression assertions passed with no test failures, warnings or skips; R startup emitted the already documented locale warnings. The steering agent did not run a new browser/Docker conformance matrix or contact the implementation agent. The checks described under SA01 and SA02 were read-only.

Recommended execution order. Finish recording any validation already in flight, then prioritize SA01-SA02 before expanding the feature matrix. Reconcile the requirement map and milestone status through SA04-SA06; use that map to select the remaining C15 work in SA07. SA08 defines the final release-evidence gate. SA03 is a separate conditional certification milestone, because the existing local implementation scope does not authorize account creation, publication or certification submission. Record the disposition of each note with implementation commits and evidence, or a concrete reason for deferral. All eight notes start pending.

Implementation status (2026-11-19). SA02’s image, acquisition and dirty-flag revalidation checks are implemented in the follow-up execution record below. SA02 now implements source snapshots, archived installation input and a clean release-source check; local and hosted acceptance is complete. SA01 now pins the available official release-v5.3.4 server and proxy images after source/digest and live plan comparison. SA01 is complete: fresh hosted smoke, Basic and Message Signing passed with verified acquisition reports and recorded timings. SA04 is partial: the requirement maps account for FAPI’s 20 client clauses, relevant network/cryptography duties, OIDC code/discovery, OAuth code/refresh/metadata, PAR/JWT client authentication and JWT/Message Signing. Direct mTLS/DPoP/resource-indicator client clauses now have a companion map. G1-G4 now have their recorded regressions; G3 adds a named Message Signing configuration assessment, while G2 retains its observed purpose-policy limits. The partial RFC 9700 map adds redirect/replay and selected attack protections; remaining inherited-security and aggregate coverage work stays open. SA06’s Keycloak follow-up now proves no-cache revalidation and rotation; C06 warm-cache acceptance remains open. SA05 now separates upstream execution from local coverage and categorized limits, with regression and retained-report validation. SA06’s milestone status now distinguishes completed public/S256 interoperability from the OIDF public variant limit; C06 warm-cache acceptance remains open. SA03 and SA07-SA08 remain pending. See the release review.

Use the implemented commands in the environment README. core, extended and fapi-signing below are historical planning aliases, not accepted current CLI profile names.

SA01 (high): Restore fresh-machine reproducibility; move this part of C16 forward. The review independently obtained an anonymous registry token and checked the locked server-image manifest. The token endpoint returned HTTP 200; the manifest for sha256:a84e164e59bba31bbca83732a8506f522a746660864da7221428bab4e3157225 returned HTTP 404. Existing cached-image runs retain their evidence, but the documented path cannot currently reproduce them on a fresh CI runner.

Follow-up availability check (2026-11-18): the official registry lists published release images. Manifest GET requests for release-v5.3.4, release-v5.3.3, release-v5.3.2, release-v5.2.4, latest and unstable all returned HTTP 200. For example, registry.gitlab.com/openid/conformance-suite:release-v5.3.4 resolved to multi-platform index sha256:dcc4bd1fb7e9c00f048a67373fe2bec5ecf9feb45a6b5d55e237e5c30e5312c6, including Linux amd64 and arm64 images. Upstream’s prebuilt Compose file uses this official registry and accepts IMAGE_TAG. The 404 concerns our exact pinned build; other official versions are available. These checks retrieved image metadata, without pulling or executing replacement images. The review has not located the exact old digest elsewhere and cannot rule out other copies.

Prioritize evaluating an available official release and a separately reviewed lock update. A verified mirror of the exact old image or a pinned source build remain alternatives. Retain digest/source correspondence checks and resolve changed modules and variants explicitly if updating the suite. Do not silently substitute a tag. Acceptance: demonstrate image acquisition and a successful preflight/API/browser smoke run on a fresh GitHub runner, then measure the selected larger jobs there. See openid_prepare_image() and the registry limitation in the environment README.

SA02 (high): Check report provenance during revalidation and identify the tested source precisely. In a retained passing Message Signing report, the review changed images.server to unrelated-image, deleted image_sources and changed checkout_dirty from false to true. Calling openid_check_report(changed, original, manifest) still returned both gate_passed = true and coverage_complete = true. The reviewed input was integration/openid/.artifacts/fapi-message-signing-20261117-235701-9cb11a881c13/evidence.json. The live runner verifies the image at startup; this finding concerns the later report validator’s incomplete provenance checks, not evidence that those live runs used a different image.

Bind report image identities to the lock and expected run context, validate the required acquisition metadata and add mutation checks for absent or substituted provenance. Define source identity for release evidence: require a clean checkout or record a reproducible source-content identity tied to the installed package and fixture bytes. A parent SHA plus a dirty flag cannot reconstruct the tested changes. Development runs may remain dirty when labeled accordingly. Acceptance: the reproduction above fails revalidation, genuine serialized reports still pass, and release aggregation rejects unidentified source changes. See openid_check_report() and openid_report_context().

SA03 (conditional, high if certification is intended): Add a concrete certification-readiness milestone after the local path. C16 currently leaves hosted comparison optional, and the closing scope statement deliberately defers formal certification. Keep that boundary explicit. If certification becomes the goal, add a separate milestone with the selected official certification profile names, hosted execution, actual hosted suite version and plan/module identities, per-test client evidence, suite exports and a reviewed submission bundle. Resolve the hosted module lists independently; never reuse pinned-local results as hosted results or assume the hosted deployment runs the pinned revision.

OIDF’s RP submission instructions require suite logs, client evidence under client-data with test-name prefixes, and a signed Certification of Conformance naming the software version and official profile. They prescribe the suite’s “Publish for certification” path. The FAPI RP testing instructions explicitly exclude local-instance results from certification submissions. The sanitized CI JSON remains useful; implement a separate evidence-generation and review path for certification packaging. Use ephemeral credentials and account for the publication of submitted logs. Acceptance for readiness: a documented, reviewable bundle-generation procedure and complete evidence mapping for every selected test. Keep account actions, publication, attestation and submission outside the currently authorized local work. Formal certification remains optional until the user chooses it.

SA04 (high): Complete the requirement-to-evidence map before expanding C15. The current scope map maps suite modules and application outcomes well, but does not yet account for every applicable normative client requirement behind the intended claims. Add rows containing the specification clause, responsible role, selected configuration, existing test/report and remaining limitation. Distinguish client duties, AS/resource server duties, deployment duties, optional features and stricter package policy.

For FAPI, review the client requirements and applicable network/cryptography sections explicitly. Include refresh and rotation support, assertion audience, browser-bound per-request PKCE, authorization-initiation protection, endpoint aliases and signing restrictions. Several already have Keycloak or unit-test evidence; link and reuse it before adding scenarios. Keep RS256-based general interoperability selections separate from claims about FAPI’s permitted signing algorithms. Acceptance: every applicable requirement for each declared claim has evidence or a named remaining gap. This matrix is an engineering safeguard, not an extra OIDF submission rule.

SA05 (medium): Separate plan completion from policy and fixture limitations. coverage_complete currently combines upstream-plan completion, stricter local policy, interoperability advisories and simulated-server limitations. Retain the raw verdicts and exact exception allowlists, but give these judgments distinct meanings in reports and documentation. In particular, consider an explicit upstream-plan-completion field alongside selected-scenario completion and additional security limitations; certification status needs its own accounting.

The encrypted-state OAuth selection executes all eleven modules but remains incomplete because of the 128-character advisory. FAPI Security Profile section 5.3.2.2 note 4 anticipates encoded state exceeding 1,000 characters, and the OIDF RP testing guide allows explained WARNING, REVIEW and SKIPPED results as well as PASSED. Keep the reference-state feature and the advisory evidence without implying that the advisory alone establishes protocol nonconformance. Likewise, the mTLS checker forces incomplete coverage partly because the simulated resource server fails to deny certificate misuse; preserve that finding while separating it from client-plan completion and client obligations. Unsigned metadata over verified TLS is also a scope description, not automatically a missing generic-FAPI requirement. Acceptance: explain each flag and report complete upstream module execution independently of additional policy or server-enforcement findings. Changes here must preserve validation and evidence requirements.

SA06 (medium): Reconcile milestone status with the newer evidence. C09 still broadly describes public-client/S256 coverage as outstanding, although C13 now exercises public clients through discovery, browser login, S256, UserInfo and refresh. Compare C13 with C09’s precise positive/negative acceptance criteria, close the overlap it satisfies and name only the remaining cases. Preserve the pinned suite’s broken public-client variant as an upstream limitation. Update C10’s opening status after the compact-state work, and reconcile the older scope table with completed mTLS and Message Signing selections. Add a short current status table at the top; retain the dated execution record as history. Current command documentation should also distinguish implemented profile names from earlier proposed aliases such as core, extended and fapi-signing.

C06’s warm-cache gap remains real. The existing Keycloak rotation test is a candidate for closing it without adding another provider fixture. Require observed cache population/use before rotation, retained cache identity and refresh after rotation, with required setup failures producing failures rather than skips. Reuse its existing rogue-signature controls. Acceptance: link the actual cacheable-provider result and its scope to C06; preserve the separate OIDF no-store results and their limitation. Do not claim closure from two fresh JWKS fetches.

SA07 (medium): Give C15 explicit browser acceptance criteria. Rejected HTTP callbacks currently retain callback query material in the address bar, and openid_http_callback_matches() requires callback_cleaned = false for those cases. Improve cleanup while preserving rejection semantics, the specific error category and credential-nonreflection checks. Update the evidence predicate with the product change and verify the resulting browser URL. See the HTTP callback collector and matcher.

The new HTTPS Form Post environments are same-site. Existing cross-site tests add useful evidence but include HTTP loopback development exceptions. Add a successful HTTPS cross-site flow and its relevant error path, or explicitly retain that deployment limitation. Reconcile the separately deferred oidcc-client-test-form-post-error module with the actual selected plan variants and existing tests. These are targeted browser improvements, not new mandatory OIDF certification profiles. Use SA04 to decide which other C15 cases remain; reuse existing fixtures before adding a mock-server dependency.

SA08 (medium): Require one identifiable final revision and durable release evidence in C16. Historical runs span different package revisions, including dirty development checkouts. They document progress but cannot collectively establish the final implementation’s full declared matrix. Choose and publish that matrix, run it against one identifiable final revision and check its aggregate completeness automatically. Preserve exact variant limits and failed attempts; a smoke selection cannot substitute for a required full plan.

The current workflows retain uploaded reports for seven days. Define durable retention for release evidence and its source/lock identities, while keeping private diagnostics and certification exports out of broad artifact uploads. Use actual GitHub runner timings to choose PR, scheduled and release tiers. Acceptance: a machine-checked aggregate report rejects missing matrix entries, mixed or unidentified source revisions and missing required evidence, and the declared release reports remain available beyond ordinary CI retention. This implements C16’s existing prohibition on merging results from different commits into a complete release claim.

End of steering-agent handoff. The original plan and implementation agent’s execution record follow unchanged. Update the status of SA01-SA08 as work lands.

Prepared 2026-11-12 against shinyOAuth commit 25318cc6488a2a98bfc83d484cbbdb3190854967 (version 0.7.0.9000). Status: implementation started. The original investigation ran no external tests. C01 supplies a working local suite preflight, and C02 supplies a validated Shiny fixture. C03 adds the suite API driver and evidence validator. C04 executes three real-browser smoke modules. C05 extends the runner to all fourteen Basic RP modules for the pinned static-registration, synchronous code-flow variant. C06 now executes all six Configuration modules, with cached-key refresh coverage still incomplete because the pinned suite’s JWKS responses prohibit storage. C07 covers the fourteen-module Form Post Basic plan in Chrome on the local cross-origin, same-site deployment. C08 covers all three client refresh modules, including identity substitution and the module’s default credential-retirement policy. C09 adds verified mirai transport for the core selections, future multisession smoke/refresh parity, confidential-client authentication selections and sequential shared-pool issuer isolation. C13 now supplies public-client discovery, S256/browser login, ID token, UserInfo and refresh interoperability, including live missing-PKCE rejection. That closes the overlapping public/S256 baseline work; the pinned suite’s broken public variant remains an OIDF capability limit. C10 includes the complete twenty-three-module OIDC/private-key-JWT/DPoP variant and eleven-module OAuth-only selections with both encrypted and reference state. All reference-state outcomes are PASSED; encrypted state retains its exact advisory. Both execute the full upstream module list, while the conservative coverage field retains the advisory separately. C11’s mTLS and C12’s Message Signing selections are implemented with the scope limits in the current table above. C13-C14 supply the second-provider scenarios recorded below; C15 browser/cryptographic follow-ups and C16 release aggregation remain.

Execution record (2026-11-12): C00 is d0b62ff; C01 is 4dee03d. C01 validated the exact server image/source correspondence, required plans, R certificate/hostname validation, Chrome certificate pinning and wrong-pin rejection, and complete owned-resource cleanup in consecutive disposable deployments on Windows/Docker Linux containers. Its 11 environment assertions pass with no failures or skips; formatting and lint checks pass. Startup reports the host’s existing C.UTF-8 locale warnings. This establishes environment readiness, not RP conformance. Chrome uses an isolated SPKI pin instead of installing a temporary root in the system trust store; the environment README records that scope adjustment.

C02 is 88517ea. It installed this checkout into an isolated R library and drove its public module/UI APIs in Chrome against a local HTTPS metadata fixture. The code/S256, nonce/state and openid-scope checks passed, a discovery issuer mismatch stopped startup, and the synthetic secret stayed out of the DOM and app logs. No token was issued and no independent client conformance verdict was collected. Follow-up validation also requires the failed setup’s private diagnostic to identify an issuer mismatch, so an unrelated app crash cannot satisfy that check. The follow-up preflight and fixture checks both passed, along with the 11 helper assertions, jarl check integration/openid, air format integration/openid --check and patch whitespace validation.

C03 is 2b06b7a. It passed 51 evidence assertions with no failures or skips. Its live API check created the pinned Basic plan, checked all module variants, retrieved a waiting module’s issuer, rejected an unknown instance and verified interruption on cancellation. Owned Docker resources were removed. Its sanitized report marks client conformance unattempted and keeps the conformance gate false.

The first C04 browser run produced three passing suite verdicts, but the local gate correctly failed because issuer/nonce errors lacked safe claim labels. 83ec40e adds those labels to the existing typed audit events without exposing claim values or changing validation. Its focused signed-token regression checks and neighboring ID-token checks passed: 162 assertions, zero failures, warnings or skips.

C04 is d723b6b. It adds the real Chrome driver, app-stop failure control, callback cleanup checks and a manual Ubuntu workflow. Two complete Windows smoke runs passed all three modules with matching app evidence and owned-resource cleanup. The evidence validator now has 54 passing assertions. Coverage remains partial; C05 is next. Preflight, API checks and all three smoke modules also passed as a non-root Linux user (R 4.5.0, Chromium 156), including caller-owned TLS key generation. The manual GitHub workflow has not run yet; its actionlint check passes, along with R lint, formatting and patch whitespace checks.

Sanitized reports retained locally under integration/openid/.artifacts/: smoke-20261112-225149-dbdbc91a7b81/evidence.json and smoke-20261112-225410-77d6e303d949/evidence.json (Windows), plus smoke-20261112-220117-83dd3e2312e6/evidence.json (Linux). Each reports a passing smoke gate, verified cleanup and incomplete full-profile coverage.

02e677e extends safe ID-token audit classification to audience, subject, issued-at, disallowed algorithms and invalid signatures. The signed-token regressions and neighboring claim checks passed 263 assertions with no failures, warnings or skips. Validation behavior remains unchanged.

C05 is c4ae74e. It executes all fourteen modules and requires the corresponding app evidence. Thirteen require FINISHED/PASSED; only oidcc-client-test-idtoken-sig-none requires FINISHED/SKIPPED, matching the pinned suite’s documented optional unsigned-token support and shinyOAuth’s disallowed_algorithm rejection. The gate also requires no UserInfo completion for rejected ID tokens. For a UserInfo subject mismatch, the typed error and suite verdict establish the UserInfo response, while the token-exchange completion audit establishes the preceding validated ID token. A UserInfo rejection can precede its completion audit; an initial Linux run caught and corrected that harness assumption.

The evidence validator passes 115 assertions, including all-module coverage, the exact unsigned-token exception and rejection-category checks. The complete Windows Basic run took 90.35 seconds for its module loop, and a later smoke run took 23.31 seconds. Those timings include per-case app/browser startup and suite waits, but exclude package installation, suite startup, the app-stop control and stack teardown. The Ubuntu workflow now runs smoke on relevant pull requests and offers Basic through manual dispatch. Full Basic stays manual until GitHub runner timings are measured; no GitHub run has executed yet.

Windows reports retained under integration/openid/.artifacts/: basic-20261112-230808-fe5a9984784b/evidence.json (complete Basic module coverage) and smoke-20261112-231056-3e4d6d264675/evidence.json (partial coverage). Both gates pass with verified owned-resource cleanup. C06 is next.

The corrected full Basic gate also passed as a non-root Linux user with R 4.5.0 and Chromium 156. Its module loop took 77.75 seconds; the retained report is integration/openid/.artifacts/basic-20261112-221342-9dbc14ec0352/evidence.json. All fourteen modules finished with their expected verdict and app evidence, the app-stop control passed, and owned-resource cleanup completed. R lint, formatting, actionlint and patch whitespace checks pass.

C06 execution: efb54a5 adds its runner coverage; 65fb2cb adds a safe discovery_issuer_mismatch audit reason and the iss claim label without changing validation. Discovery and neighboring JWKS tests passed 234 assertions with no failures, warnings or skips. The runner now resolves separate Basic/Configuration plans, verifies the exact six-module Configuration list and schedules both upstream-ignored rotation modules. Discovery-only results earn no login credit. A failed discovery setup must identify the expected issuer check through typed audit evidence.

The first live Configuration run completed all six suite modules, but its local gate rejected the cache evidence. A separate module confirmed that JWKS is sent with Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, max-age=0, must-revalidate. shinyOAuth correctly leaves those keys unstored. No suite headers, response bodies, assertions or client cache policy were changed to force a warm cache. The recorded limitation is suite_jwks_no_store_prevents_cached_key_refresh_test.

The before-signing scenario prefetches through the installed package’s internal JWKS helper, then requires a validated token with a different signing-key ID. The repeated-login scenario requires two validated ID-token/UserInfo outcomes, different key IDs, a local logout between them and the same R app/cache instances throughout. Only key-ID digests leave the fixture. The driver waits for the next callback session, which prevents a logged-out state from satisfying the second-login wait. The evidence validator passes 168 assertions; focused HTTP-cache, invalidation, signature and refresh-throttle regressions add 74 passing assertions with no failures, warnings or skips.

Configuration gates pass on Windows (R 4.5.1, Chrome 157) and non-root Linux (R 4.5.0, Chromium 156): five modules are FINISHED/PASSED, and unsigned-token rejection is FINISHED/SKIPPED under its existing optional policy. Both runs verify owned-resource cleanup. Their module loops took 38.35 and 29.79 seconds. Sanitized reports retained under integration/openid/.artifacts/ are config-20261112-233608-c8bf6297fde2/evidence.json (Windows) and config-20261112-223608-312b32a78ab4/evidence.json (Linux). Manifest and client-evidence schemas are now version 2. Manual workflow dispatch offers config; pull requests continue to run smoke. The full Basic profile also passed again on non-root Linux after the plan and driver changes, with all fourteen expected module outcomes and complete Basic coverage. Its retained schema-2 report is integration/openid/.artifacts/basic-20261112-223754-36fbb02417e4/evidence.json; the module loop took 80.85 seconds. R lint, formatting, actionlint and patch whitespace checks pass. No owned suite containers remain after validation.

C06 acceptance remains partial: reports keep selection_complete = true, coverage_complete = false and cached_key_refresh_tested = false, even if the manifest accidentally requests a complete-coverage label. A follow-up must test warm-cache key replacement against an independent cacheable provider (an applicable Keycloak scenario or C13’s second provider), or a reviewed suite configuration/version that permits caching. Preserve the current no-store runs as their own evidence. C07’s form-post work can proceed independently; the first OIDC milestone retains this C06 coverage gap until that follow-up passes.

C07 is 20966df2. C07 execution (2026-11-13): the pinned Form Post Basic plan resolves to the fourteen Basic modules with its fixed response_mode=form_post variant. The runner installs the normal Form Post wrapper and records sanitized Chrome navigation evidence separately from incoming POST metadata. Every case must show GET authorization, a form-encoded callback POST from the expected provider Origin, the 303 bridge redirect, Secure SameSite=Strict binding-cookie metadata, completed callback validation and final callback-query cleanup. No raw request/response bodies, callback queries or cookie values are retained.

The full profile passes on Windows (R 4.5.1, Chrome 157) and non-root Linux (R 4.5.0, Chromium 156): thirteen FINISHED/PASSED verdicts and the documented unsigned-token FINISHED/SKIPPED, with matching app outcomes and verified cleanup. Module loops took 103.27 and 81.54 seconds. Retained sanitized reports under integration/openid/.artifacts/ are form-post-20261113-205121-e013f0e3cb20/evidence.json (Windows) and form-post-20261113-195207-4bded3721513/evidence.json (Linux). Their actual provider/app origins were https://localhost:59182 / https://localhost:60189 and https://localhost:59345 / https://localhost:41039, respectively. Chrome observed same-site on every callback, so cross_origin = true and cross_site = false. This scope does not replace the separate cross-site attack fixtures.

The evidence validator passes 208 assertions, including rejection of missing POST/bridge/binding observations, stale origins, wrong transports and incorrect site labels. Existing Form Post response-mode, module-transport and candidate storage regressions passed 532 assertions with no failures, warnings or skips. The query-callback smoke selection also passed again on Windows, with its partial-coverage flag and cleanup intact. Its report is integration/openid/.artifacts/smoke-20261113-205453-266a10a4126f/evidence.json; the module loop took 22.91 seconds. R lint, formatting, actionlint and patch whitespace checks pass. Manual workflow dispatch now offers form-post; pull requests continue to run smoke. The upstream Form Post Basic plan does not select the separate oidcc-client-test-form-post-error module; comprehensive-plan coverage remains a C09 task. The C06 warm-cache gap remains open.

C08 is 3c7aa049. C08 execution (2026-11-13): the pinned client refresh plan resolves to three modules with no forced per-module variants. A live API probe established that the plan uses JSON null for those variants. The driver omits the optional runner variant parameter for those entries and still requires the complete plan variant in every runtime result.

Each case completes a normal browser login, retains the original grant and validated identity in the same app and Shiny session, then explicitly calls the public connection’s $refresh() method. The positive case retains the original ID token, issuer, subject and connection, fetches UserInfo during refresh, and exports the new access token through $access_token(). The two negative cases require an ID-token audit error naming iss or sub, the normal token_refresh_error, session clearing, an unusable retained connection and blocked access-token export. Their UserInfo count stays at the initial login’s one request. The fixture does not log out or modify token state to produce those outcomes. Reports contain comparison booleans and counts, without identity or credential values.

The changed-subject rejection already existed; diagnostic commit bfe4fdf8 adds its missing safe claim label. The signed-claim audit, refresh issuer/audience and rejected-refresh cleanup regressions pass 321 assertions with no failures, warnings or skips. The expanded evidence validator passes 307 assertions, including attempts to pass with missing grants, new sessions/apps, absent checkpoints, wrong operation counts or incomplete retirement evidence.

All three modules finish FINISHED/PASSED on Windows (R 4.5.1, Chrome 157) and non-root Linux (R 4.5.0, Chromium 156), with matching app outcomes, the real-app failure control and verified cleanup. The module loops took 25.53 and 22.96 seconds. Retained sanitized reports are integration/openid/.artifacts/refresh-20261113-222805-fd5b072e2f42/evidence.json (Windows) and integration/openid/.artifacts/refresh-20261113-212915-8f51a2246236/evidence.json (Linux). Both record the C08 working tree based on bfe4fdf8 with checkout_dirty = true. Each reports complete coverage for this exact synchronous, static-registration, code-flow refresh plan with query callbacks and HTTP Basic client authentication. The upstream refresh plan is outside certification.

The query-callback smoke selection passes again with partial coverage and verified cleanup; its report is integration/openid/.artifacts/smoke-20261113-222936-bd3794b1ce39/evidence.json. R lint, formatting, actionlint and patch whitespace checks pass.

Manual workflow dispatch now offers refresh and uploads only its sanitized evidence files. Pull requests continue to select smoke. The GitHub workflow has not run yet. Further C09 work follows below; C06’s warm-cache gap remains open, and rotation/concurrency/retained-connection regressions remain separate evidence layers.

C09, first slice (2026-11-13): all core selections accept --transport mirai. Future multisession is limited to smoke and refresh parity selections; other future profile combinations fail explicitly. Each module case starts its own two-worker pool and checks backend selection. Both workers must load the private checkout namespace, make a verified HTTPS request to /api/server using the temporary CA and reject a wrong hostname. These setup probes do not earn protocol coverage. Actual token/UserInfo and validation-error events must come from the observed worker PIDs, with the matching package version and CA setting. Main-only execution cannot satisfy an async selection.

The fixture’s audit hook now writes only sanitized, allowlisted metadata to atomic per-event files. The main app aggregates process-specific operation counts and safe claim/error labels. Every event stays bound to its run and package installation, while credentials, identities, error messages and paths stay out of those records. Refresh waits for its promise before checking identity continuity, token export and credential retirement. Evidence schema 3 requires these transport checks and verified process cleanup; the profile manifest remains schema 2. The validator passes 363 assertions with no failures, warnings or skips, including rejection of fallback execution, missing/foreign worker PIDs, stale installations, failed TLS probes and absent cleanup.

The app registers exit handlers for its worker pool. Linux first interrupts the app and permits orderly shutdown; forced termination remains a fallback. Cleanup checks both descendants and the specifically observed worker PIDs. Docker-hosted drivers need --init to reap orphaned workers; a bare R process as container PID 1 left zombie entries and correctly failed the strict check. The browser has an explicit temporary profile, a 30-second startup budget and an observed close-command promise. Browser process termination remains required. Native websocket EOF messages can appear during intentional browser shutdown. Browser/port fixes are in the separate harness commit 9b287959. The suite now publishes random loopback ports in 20000-45000: Linux-side port probes could not see Windows Docker Desktop’s excluded dynamic-port ranges, which caused real bind failures in the earlier 49152-65535 range.

Manual dispatch now selects the transport and installs the worker dependencies. Pull requests retain synchronous smoke; hosted CI timings remain unmeasured. Configuration keeps coverage_complete = false in every transport. Its main cache template is retained, while async dispatch serializes worker copies; the report records that scope and does not claim a shared warm cache.

The complete Basic, Form Post Basic, Configuration and refresh selections pass with mirai on Windows (R 4.5.1, Chrome 157, mirai 2.7.1) and non-root Linux (R 4.5.0, Chromium 156, mirai 2.7.4). C09, confidential-client slice (completed 2026-11-16): auth-post, auth-secret-jwt and auth-private-jwt select two modules each from the pinned Comprehensive plan: the normal login and invalid-issuer modules. The resolved code-flow lists contain twenty-nine modules for shared-secret authentication and twenty-eight for private-key JWT; the manifest freezes those lists and requires their null per-module variants. These selections stay partial and the upstream plan is non-certifiable.

Static registration declares the selected method, with fresh credentials per plan. Secret JWT uses HS256; private-key JWT uses RS256 with a fresh RSA key and public-only JWKS registration. The app receives the private PEM and uses normal public discovery, client and module APIs. Sync and mirai must each produce a validated ID-token/UserInfo login and a typed issuer rejection, with no retained rejected identity or UserInfo request after that rejection.

The evidence helper reads the suite’s recorded HTTP requests and authentication condition results. It requires the actual expected method, matching client IDs, no mixed authentication mechanisms, correct secret or JWT metadata, and successful credential/signature and claim checks from the suite. Sensitive values are compared only in memory. Raw logs, secrets, assertions, private keys, codes and claim values stay out of the report. Evidence tests cover stale instance/probe identities, wrong credentials, mixed auth, invalid PKCE, bad assertion metadata and accidental disclosure. All 547 assertions pass with no failures, warnings or skips.

Two pinned-suite gaps remain explicit. The public-client variant still omits none from discovery and its public authentication sequence performs no checks. A separate disposable probe confirms the missing advertised method and the installed package’s typed discovery rejection. The probe is cancelled and earns no conformance credit; public_client_authentication_tested = false. Metadata and discovery policy remain unchanged.

The client base class also guards verifier validation with env.containsObject("code_challenge"), while the challenge condition stores a string. Consequently the pinned code-flow client plan skips its verifier check. The companion helper requires the suite’s S256 challenge-presence check and independently computes the challenge from the actual token-request verifier. It retains suite_pkce_verifier_checked = false and a coverage limitation. This establishes matching client requests; bad-verifier rejection still needs an enforcing provider. The scope record links the exact pinned source and describes the limits.

C09, shared-pool slice (2026-11-16): run-shared-pool.R keeps one R process and two verified mirai workers alive across eight alternating browser flows. POST and private-key-JWT clients each complete a normal login and a typed issuer rejection, then repeat with fresh registrations and credentials. Each plan has a distinct discovered issuer, shared by its two modules. Each case gets a new app, client and cache object, while the process and worker identities must stay the same. The gate requires an observed worker to perform protocol work for both methods; merely starting a pool cannot establish reuse.

Four nested selections retain the existing authentication evidence gates, including actual request comparisons, S256, suite authentication checks and typed issuer rejection. The aggregate gate binds the plan/module identities and execution order. Different audit hooks and timeout settings must reach protocol work. Both workers are inspected before and after every case for restored hook/timeout options and empty async session context. Earlier audit files must remain unchanged after later cases. Cleanup credit stays false until the shared process and observed workers stop. The first live attempt caught a fixture handoff bug: a completed case’s stop signal could end the next app. The fixture now closes its session and retires that signal before the next handoff, and an unrequested app stop fails immediately.

This checks sequential reuse, including returning to both authentication methods with new credentials after the first rejected logins. Concurrent multi-issuer dispatch, shared cache objects and other auth pairings remain outside this selection. Reports keep partial coverage and the existing suite public-client and PKCE limitations. The manual workflow exposes shared-pool with mirai and uploads only its sanitized root report. Registry availability still blocks a fresh hosted run.

Commit d3736366 adds the explicit id_token_profile = "fapi2" discovery policy. The first live attempt exposed the mismatch between standard OIDC’s RS256 discovery requirement and FAPI’s permitted signing algorithms. The new policy keeps normal issuer, endpoint, JWKS and metadata validation, and intersects implemented FAPI algorithms with the caller and advertised sets. Standard OIDC still requires RS256. PS256-only metadata has no supported algorithm overlap. The discovery fix passed 367 focused assertions with zero test failures, warnings or skips, including the existing standard OIDC cases.

The fixture supplies separate ephemeral ES256 server, client-authentication and DPoP keys through the normal suite/provider configuration. Client registration contains only its public key. Normal discovery selects DPoP token types and the existing minimal front-channel mode; compatibility mode’s extra browser parameters correctly failed the first suite run. Client assertions use the discovered issuer as a string audience. The app validates its ID token and UserInfo before explicitly requesting the exported accounts endpoint through the public connection API. HTTP 200 and the suite’s completion marker are required; UserInfo alone cannot satisfy resource coverage.

Evidence compares actual PAR, token, UserInfo and accounts requests in memory. It requires ES256 assertions, correct S256, only client ID/request URI at the authorization endpoint, DPoP method/URI/key consistency, distinct JTIs and the resource access-token hash. Nonce cases require observed repeated requests with changed nonces and the suite’s successful nonce checks. The no-nonce case requires one request at each endpoint and absent proof nonces. The suite’s verifier-matching condition runs in this plan; the separate OIDC-plan PKCE limitation remains unchanged. Invalid ID-token issuer handling must retain no token and make no UserInfo or accounts call.

Login executes in the chosen sync/mirai transport. The connection’s imperative resource request runs in the Shiny process, and reports record that PID and scope. Raw logs, assertions, proofs, keys, credential values and response bodies stay out of uploaded reports. Manual CI offers this selection; fresh hosted execution still needs the pinned server image to become available.

The malformed callbacks are rejected by the public UI’s HTTP handler before a callback Shiny session starts. The driver therefore collects the actual browser HTTP 400 response instead of waiting for a second Shiny snapshot. Its evidence requires the matching allowlisted audit label, response body match, no-store, no-referrer, plain text and no reflected credentials. No token exchange, UserInfo or accounts request is allowed, and this stage earns no authentication or worker protocol-work credit. Discovery rejection likewise earns only discovery-stage evidence. Malformed-callback error pages retain their query in the address bar; reports explicitly record callback_cleaned = false for those four cases. Other callback paths still require URL cleanup. C15 should revisit query retention on these HTTP error pages as a separate privacy improvement, while preserving rejection and preventing reflection of callback credentials.

Three isolated attacker instances use the real issued token with a wrong certificate, a wrong certificate plus a forged certificate header, and no certificate. All three must produce the expected certificate-failure verdict and independently observed unexpected TLS peer. They use a raw attacker request, with a separate report label from the normal connection request. Their IDs, full variants, run/attempt/checkout/source/plan identity, application outcome, worker execution and cleanup must match this run. They receive no normal-module pass credit.

These controls establish a limitation in the pinned suite. Its checkMtlsCertificate() continues after EnsureClientCertificateMatches fails. Wrong-certificate and forged-header attempts therefore return HTTP 200 with the resource marker while the suite marks their instances FAILED. Missing certificates return HTTP 400 and INTERRUPTED/FAILED. The harness preserves those outcomes and always forces coverage_complete = false with mtls_resource_denial_not_established, including if the manifest’s complete flag or coverage limits are changed. The upstream suite remains unchanged.

C11’s independent resource-denial check is implemented in df714b2c. It extends the existing Python strict-AS fixture with a protected resource. The resource records the actual TLS peer certificate for each issued token and compares it with the resource request’s TLS peer. Two eligible certificates have identical subject names but different DER encodings; a token issued to either certificate requires that particular certificate.

Each platform completes 32 bound grants across RS256/RS384 JAR and private-key-JWT authentication, direct authorization/PAR, sync/mirai token callbacks, returned/omitted cnf, and both certificates. Public Shiny module and connection APIs perform the exchange and resource request. Wrong or missing certificates, forged certificate headers, unknown tokens and two additional unbound grants produce 162 actual HTTP 401 responses per platform, with invalid_token, a Bearer challenge and no resource content. The rightful holder can still access the resource afterward, including with a misleading certificate header.

The runner installs the checkout in a private library and verifies that both the main process and callback workers load that installation. Exchange counts and process IDs distinguish sync from mirai execution. CI uploads only sanitized JSON reports containing revision, dirty flag, dependency versions, installation checks and assertion counts; private libraries, keys and logs are excluded.

Compact JWTs, claim values, signing keys, codes and raw HTTP error text stay private. C14 resource-indicator implementation (2026-11-18): a separate resources selection adds native RFC 8707 behavior for two API audiences and a rejected unknown resource. It uses confidential Basic authentication, direct query authorization and S256. PAR is explicitly disabled for this selection. Chrome must observe the exact resource parameter in the outgoing request; native authorization, code and refresh events must confirm the same indicator. Both APIs must obtain their own audience and the resource-specific api.read scope through the provider’s normal resource-indicator processing. Consent uses the public Grant API for resource scopes; no protocol handler is patched.

Each positive case validates its ID token, uses connection$request() at the selected API, refreshes the same connection and uses the refreshed credential at that API. Native introspection confirms the current token’s audience and scope before and after refresh. The original validated identity must survive the native refresh response without a replacement ID token. Native UserInfo is disabled because it rejects API-audience tokens. The package’s scope policy remains enabled; its warning about API access-token scope omitting OIDC/offline scopes is expected here. The harness independently requires api.read and validated ID-token identity.

The resource server is a development fixture on two HTTPS paths sharing the provider’s origin. It checks opaque-token validity, audience and scope through the provider’s public AccessToken/Grant model API. It is not an independent resource-server product or a JWT access-token verifier. Native provider handlers validate indicators and mint audiences. A real token for the other API, absent credentials and an invalid token must receive HTTP 401. The public connection must also reject an escaped resource base locally, with no extra server request. The unknown indicator must produce native invalid_target and the matching client callback error before code or token issuance.

Each report requires all three browser cases, the stopped-app canary, real sync/mirai exchange and refresh, owned-worker cleanup, complete provider events, two authenticated resource reads and introspections per positive case, and the three denial probes. Serialized reports and altered evidence must also be checked; missing or false control results cannot pass. Only sanitized evidence JSON is eligible for upload. Manual workflow dispatch now offers resources alongside basic and advanced; pull requests keep basic sync.

C14 browser-retention implementation (2026-11-18): the retention selection adds query and Form Post cases using oauth_connections_server() against the unmodified pinned provider. A browser owner, one client and the encrypted memory store persist outside the Shiny server function. After native OIDC login the browser loads a second page and returns through full document navigation. New Shiny sessions must restore the same connection ID and validated identity in the same R process; each session obtains a new connection reference. Four public resource requests use native UserInfo, including before/after refresh and after both navigations. The public identity() API verifies ID-token and UserInfo continuity, with only a salted identity digest retained in reports.

Each case also opens a separate Chrome profile. That browser must have no saved connection and must receive the typed unavailable-connection error when probing the other owner’s ID. Local logout (revoke = FALSE, reload = FALSE) must make the old R reference unusable and block token export. After a full reload, the new empty owner must also reject the old ID. The test makes no remote revocation claim for this action; advanced interoperability covers revocation separately. Cookie evidence requires one Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax owner cookie at the root path, unavailable to JavaScript, without retaining its value.

Evidence requires exact native events: the missing-PKCE rejection, one code exchange, one refresh and six successful current-token UserInfo calls. This prevents a new authorization from substituting for restoration. It also checks the complete snapshot sequence, new session counters, stable app/process/ID, identity comparisons, live denial outcomes and explicit cleanup. Every report has a stopped-managed-app canary, altered-evidence checks and serialized report validation, including rejection of missing or false control results. Form Post uses the real POST and HTTP 303 bridge.

The selected sync/mirai transport handles exchange, refresh and validated UserInfo. Explicit resource reads, owner checks and memory-store updates stay in the main process. Both origins use HTTPS localhost on different ports; cross-site cookie deployments, account owners, expiry, multiple clients, sender-bound grants and process restarts remain outside this selection. The existing synthetic retention fixtures continue to cover their own scope. Manual dispatch now offers retention, uploading only sanitized evidence JSON.

SA04 JWT regression G1 (2026-11-19): the new encrypted-JARM regression covers both query.jwt module callbacks and the form_post.jwt admission bridge. It encrypts a correctly formed inner response whose real RS256 signature has one altered byte, or whose inner algorithm/signature has been changed to none. Each case first proves successful authenticated outer decryption, then requires the specific inner rejection, no authenticated session/token, zero token-endpoint HTTP calls and the exact pending state record/keys unchanged. The original correctly signed response then completes one exchange and consumes that same state. The 68 new assertions exercise actual decryption, JWKS selection, signature verification and module/bridge handling; only HTTP responses are stubbed. This is unit/module coverage with an explicit browser-marker bypass, not a real browser or encrypted OIDF profile result. No runtime defect was found.

The new cases plus existing JARM response/compression regressions passed 864 assertions on each of Windows and Linux, including the 68 new assertions, with zero failures, test warnings or skips. The first Linux check correctly failed its zero-skip requirement when an existing Ed25519 case lacked optional sodium; the accepted disposable container supplied the system library and private R package without changing the base image or package dependencies. Formatting, jarl, whitespace and independent review passed. G1 is complete as a focused regression; G2-G4 and the broader source-qualified release matrix remain open.

SA04 JWT regression G4 (2026-11-19): a new real-signature corpus exercises ID-token/JARM module callbacks and public signed-UserInfo retrieval. Eight cases per context include ordinary signed positives, valid optional jku/x5u headers, attacker-signed JWTs pointing to attacker keys, unmatched SQL/path-shaped key IDs and correctly registered literal unusual-key-ID positives. The only mock is httr2::req_perform(); every HTTP destination is recorded, and attacker locations would supply matching attacker keys if requested. No header-selected location is contacted. Trusted provider JWKS still supplies the verification keys, unknown IDs fail and registered literal IDs remain usable.

Rejected JARM keeps the pending state and makes no token request. Rejected ID tokens stop UserInfo/authentication after the required token response. Invalid signed UserInfo returns no claims. Windows and Linux each passed 274 focused locator/JWKS/JOSE assertions, including 171 new assertions, with zero failures, test warnings or skips; formatting, jarl and whitespace checks passed. Private result CSVs/RDS remain under ignored codex/jwt-untrusted-locators/. This is unit/module evidence with an explicit browser-marker bypass, not a browser, filesystem/SQL audit or new OIDF execution. No runtime defect was found. G1/G4 are now covered; G2/G3 and the complete source-qualified release matrix remain open.

SA04 PAR and JWT-authentication map (2026-11-19): the new direct-clause map accounts for eight grouped PAR and nine JWT client-authentication duties from RFC 9126, RFC 7521 and RFC 7523. Mapping a duty does not establish a new execution or close the overall SA04/release matrix.

That audit identified a concrete independent-fixture error: invalid client assertions reached the generic invalid_request handler. The strict AS now classifies assertion parsing/claim failures, invalid signatures and competing credentials as invalid_client, with a specific signature reason. The assertion-profile rule in RFC 7521 section 4.2.1 is kept distinct from generic OAuth error wording. Request Object and unrelated grant processing stay outside the authentication boundary; the existing unknown-code invalid_request / invalid_code behavior is explicitly retained as a separate fixture limitation.

The new real-HTTPS regression deliberately expires correctly signed RS256 and RS384 client-authentication assertions at PAR and token endpoints, verifies the signatures independently, and checks exact denial bodies/headers. Failed PAR registers no pending state or usable reference; failed token exchange consumes the callback state and blocks replay without another request. Neither path retains an authenticated token or connection. Fresh assertions and a new public preparation then succeed against the same server. Separate controls cover invalid signatures, competing nonempty credentials, expired Request Objects and unknown codes.

Windows and Linux each passed 111 assertions across five focused cases, with zero failures, errors, test warnings or skips.
